title: Richard Socher's Recursive Superintelligence Signs $410 Million AWS Compute Deal to Scale Self-Improving AI
excerpt: The London-based AI lab, which raised $650 million in May at a $4.65 billion valuation, will use Amazon Web Services infrastructure to power its quest for recursively self-improving artificial intelligence.
body:
• Recursive Superintelligence has signed a $410 million, multi-year compute deal with Amazon Web Services to scale its self-improving AI systems
  • The company raised $650 million in May at a $4.65 billion valuation, led by Google's GV and Greycroft, with participation from Nvidia and AMD Ventures
  • Founded by former Salesforce Chief Scientist Richard Socher, the lab is building AI that can autonomously identify its own weaknesses and redesign itself
  • The team of more than 25 researchers includes veterans from Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Meta AI, and Uber AI, operating from San Francisco and London
  • The deal underscores the massive capital requirements of frontier AI research, with compute emerging as the critical bottleneck for ambitious labs

A Massive Bet on Self-Improving AI

Recursive Superintelligence, the AI lab founded by former Salesforce Chief Scientist Richard Socher, announced on Tuesday a $410 million, multi-year compute deal with Amazon Web Services. The agreement gives the London-headquartered startup access to AWS cloud infrastructure to power its ambitious mission: building artificial intelligence that can recursively improve itself without human intervention.

The deal comes just two months after Recursive emerged from stealth with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, in a round led by Google's venture arm GV and Greycroft, with chipmakers Nvidia and AMD also investing. The AWS commitment means Recursive will deploy the majority of its raised capital on compute infrastructure — a pattern increasingly common among frontier AI labs where raw processing power has become the primary constraint.

The Team and the Vision

Socher, who is best known for his work on ImageNet and for founding the early AI search startup You.com, has assembled a formidable research team. Co-founders include Tim Rocktäschel, a professor of AI at University College London and former Google DeepMind scientist, alongside Jeff Clune, Josh Tobin, Tim Shi, and the legendary AI researcher Peter Norvig. The team of more than 25 researchers and engineers operates from offices in San Francisco and London.

The company's core thesis is that the fastest path to superintelligent AI runs through systems that can improve themselves. Rather than simply training larger models on more data, Recursive aims to build AI that can autonomously generate research ideas, implement and test them, and validate the results — an automated loop of scientific discovery that the company compares to biological evolution.

"Our main focus is to build truly recursive, self-improving superintelligence at scale, which means that the entire process of ideation, implementation, and validation of research ideas would be automatic."

— Richard Socher, CEO, Recursive Superintelligence

Context and Competition

Recursive sits within a rapidly growing cohort of frontier AI labs pursuing self-improving intelligence. Safe Superintelligence, Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab, Yann LeCun's AMI Labs, and David Silver's Ineffable Intelligence are all pursuing variations on the same theme, collectively attracting tens of billions of dollars in venture capital. The 2026 frontier AI capital cycle has produced roughly a dozen "team-only" labs raising in the $1 billion to $5 billion range without a commercial product.

The AWS deal also highlights the growing entanglement between cloud providers and AI labs. Amazon has committed $13 billion to Anthropic, with a potential total commitment of up to $33 billion, including a 10-year AWS deal worth $100 billion. Microsoft has poured over $13 billion into OpenAI. For AWS, deals with smaller labs like Recursive help diversify its AI customer base beyond its anchor investment in Anthropic.

What It Means for India's AI Ecosystem

For India's burgeoning AI sector, the scale of capital flowing into frontier research labs raises both competitive and collaborative questions. Socher's lab has no announced India operations, but the company's London-San Francisco structure and its reliance on researchers from global institutions like UCL suggest potential future ties to India's deep bench of AI talent. Indian engineers and researchers have been prominent in the founding teams of several recent frontier AI startups.

More broadly, the race to build self-improving AI has implications for India's own AI ambitions. The Indian government's IndiaAI initiative and private-sector investments by companies like Reliance, Tata, and Infosys are focused primarily on AI applications rather than frontier research. The scale of compute spending by labs like Recursive — which is committing nearly two-thirds of its total funding to cloud infrastructure alone — illustrates the enormous financial barriers to entry in the frontier AI race.

What's Next

Recursive has targeted a public product launch by mid-2026. The company says its approach, which it calls "open-ended" self-improvement, uses co-evolving competing AI agents that continuously challenge and refine one another across millions of iterations. Whether this vision can translate into a working product — or remains an expensive research endeavor — will be one of the defining tests of the current AI investment cycle.
